title: Segmented Sieve
directAnswer: You want primes in a high window [L, R] where R can be up to 10¹² but R−L is small. A plain sieve of size R won't fit in memory. The fix: sieve normally up to √R to get the 'base primes', then use only those base primes to cross out composites inside a boolean window of size R−L+1. Any composite x in [L, R] has a prime factor ≤ √x ≤ √R, so the base primes are enough to mark every composite in the window. Time is O((R−L) log log R + √R log log √R), memory is O(R−L + √R).

remember.pattern: Sieve base primes up to √R, then cross out their multiples inside the window [L, R]
remember.formula:
base = primesUpTo(floor(sqrt(R)))   # plain sieve
mark = [True] * (R - L + 1)            # index i ↔ number L+i
for p in base:
    start = max(p*p, ((L + p - 1) // p) * p)   # first multiple of p ≥ L, but ≥ p*p
    for m from start to R step p:
        mark[m - L] = False
if L == 1: mark[0] = False   # 1 is not prime
primes = [L + i for i, ok in enumerate(mark) if ok]
rules: The base primes only need to reach **√R**, never R — that is the whole point and the reason the window fits in memory.
Offset every window index by L: number `x` lives at `mark[x − L]`. Forgetting the `− L` shift is the signature bug of this problem.
Start crossing out p's multiples at `max(p*p, first multiple of p ≥ L)` — and compute that first multiple as `ceil(L / p) * p`, not by scanning.
Handle `L == 1` explicitly: 1 is not prime but no base prime crosses it out, so it leaks into the result unless you clear `mark[0]`.
Use **long** for `p*p` and for the multiple arithmetic in Java — with R near 10¹² these products overflow a 32-bit int.
whenToUse: You need every prime in a **high range** [L, R] where R is far too large to sieve directly
The window width R − L is small (fits in memory) even though R itself is huge
You already need a √R base sieve and just want to extend it to a shifted window
Counting or listing primes in [L, R] for number-theory queries
antiSignals: You need all primes from 2 up to a modest n → the plain Sieve of Eratosthenes is simpler
You only need to test **one** number for primality → trial division to √x or Miller–Rabin
The window R − L itself is enormous (also ~10¹²) → no boolean window fits; you need a different idea
R is small (≤ 10⁷) → just sieve directly, no segmentation needed
remember.takeaway: The segmented sieve is the plain sieve with one realisation: a composite in [L, R] is betrayed by a prime factor no larger than √R, so you never need primes beyond √R to clean the window. Precompute those base primes once, slide them across a size-(R−L) boolean buffer, and you sieve ranges that would never fit if addressed from 0. The index shift `x → x − L` and the `L == 1` special case are the two details that decide whether your code is correct.

interviewerIntent.testing: Whether you realise that primes up to √R are sufficient to sieve any window ending at R, and whether you can map a number x to its slot x − L in a shifted boolean array without off-by-one errors.
interviewerIntent.commonMistake: Trying to allocate a boolean array of size R (out of memory for R ~ 10¹²), forgetting the x − L index shift, or mishandling L = 1 so that 1 is reported as prime.
interviewerIntent.toStandOut: State the invariant out loud — 'every composite ≤ R has a prime factor ≤ √R' — then derive that the base sieve only needs √R, and compute the first in-window multiple as ceil(L/p)·p instead of looping up from p.

problemStatement:
Given two integers `L` and `R` (with `L ≤ R`), return all prime numbers in the inclusive range `[L, R]` in increasing order.

The upper bound `R` can be as large as about `10¹²`, but the window width `R − L` is small (say up to `10⁶`). A standard sieve sized to `R` would not fit in memory, so you must sieve the window directly using only the primes up to `√R`.
constraints: 1 ≤ L ≤ R ≤ 10¹² (R is huge; R − L is the part that fits in memory)
0 ≤ R − L ≤ 10⁶ (window width — the boolean buffer is O(R − L))
L may equal 1 → 1 is not prime and must be excluded
understanding: We are not asked for all primes up to R — only those in a narrow band [L, R] that sits high on the number line. The key fact: if a number x ≤ R is composite, it has a prime factor at most √x ≤ √R. So the primes up to √R are enough 'erasers' to cross out every composite in the window. We sieve those base primes once with a plain sieve, then carry a boolean array indexed by offset from L and let each base prime cross out its multiples that fall inside [L, R].

clarifyingQuestions.question: How large can R get, and how wide is the window R − L?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: R can be ~10¹² (too big to sieve directly), but R − L fits in memory (≤ 10⁶). That gap is exactly why we segment: base primes up to √R, window buffer of size R − L.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Is the range inclusive of both L and R?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Yes, [L, R] inclusive. Index x maps to slot x − L, so the buffer has R − L + 1 entries.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Can L be 1 (or 0)?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: L can be 1. 1 is not prime, and no base prime ever crosses it out, so I clear its slot explicitly. If L were 0 I'd also clear slot 0 and 1.

clarifyingQuestions.question: Do you want the primes themselves or just the count?
clarifyingQuestions.answer: Either — the sieve is identical. I collect the survivors for the list, or tally them for a count query.

examples.explanation: Base primes up to √20 ≈ 4 are {2, 3}. They cross out 10,12,14,16,18,20 (multiples of 2) and 12,15,18 (multiples of 3) inside the window; 11,13,17,19 survive.
Same as a normal sieve over [1,10]; slot for 1 is cleared explicitly because no prime crosses it out.
Base primes up to √110 ≈ 10 are {2,3,5,7}. After crossing out their multiples in [100,110], four primes remain.

approaches.name: Sieve Everything Up To R (Baseline)
approaches.whenToMention: Mention first to expose why the obvious idea fails — it anchors the memory problem the segmented sieve solves.
hints: The most direct idea: run a normal Sieve of Eratosthenes up to R, then read off the primes that happen to fall in [L, R]. What goes wrong when R is 10¹²?
A boolean array of size R + 1 needs about R bytes. For R = 10¹² that's a terabyte — it simply will not allocate.
We don't actually need primality for every number up to R, only for the R − L numbers in the window. Can we restrict the work to that band?
approaches.complexityReasoning: A full sieve up to R does O(R log log R) crossing-out work and allocates an O(R) boolean array. The time is fine asymptotically, but the O(R) space is the killer: for R near 10¹² the array cannot fit in memory.
approaches.explanation:
The literal reading of 'primes in [L, R]' is: sieve all primes up to R the usual way, then keep the ones that land in the window. Allocate `isPrime[0..R]`, cross out multiples of each prime, and finally collect indices in `[L, R]`.

**Why it is correct.** It is just the plain Sieve of Eratosthenes followed by a range filter. Correctness is inherited directly from the standard sieve: every composite ≤ R gets crossed out, every prime survives, and we report only those in `[L, R]`.

**Why it does not ship.** The fatal flaw is space, not time. The boolean array has `R + 1` entries. With `R` around `10¹²` that is on the order of a terabyte of memory — the allocation fails before the algorithm even starts. Even when `R` is merely `10⁹`, you are burning a gigabyte to discard all but a thin slice of it. We are computing primality for `10¹²` numbers when the question only asked about the `10⁶` in the window.

**The wasted-work insight.** Almost all of the array — every index outside `[L, R]` — is computed and then thrown away. That mismatch between work done and answer needed is the signal to segment: bring the sieve to the window instead of bringing the window to a full sieve.
approaches.insight: This baseline is correct and is the right tool when R is small (say ≤ 10⁷). It fails for large R purely on memory: you allocate O(R) but only O(R − L) of it matters. Recognising that mismatch is what motivates sieving only the window.

dryRun.intro: For tiny R this works fine — sieve up to 20, then keep [10, 20]. The point is only that the array scales with R, not R − L.

Casting R to int for the array size — overflows when R exceeds 2³¹.
Believing it's 'fast enough' because the time bound looks fine — the blocker is space, not time.

approaches.name: Segmented Sieve (Optimal)
approaches.whenToMention: The answer they want for primes in a high window. Lead with 'a composite ≤ R has a prime factor ≤ √R, so I only sieve base primes up to √R'.

complexity.time: O((R − L) log log R + √R log log √R)

hints: Every composite number x has a prime factor no bigger than √x. If x ≤ R, that factor is ≤ √R. What does that tell you about which primes you actually need to cross out composites in [L, R]?
Step 1: run an ordinary sieve up to √R to get the 'base primes'. Step 2: make a boolean window of size R − L + 1 where slot i represents the number L + i.
For each base prime p, find the first multiple of p that is ≥ L (use ceil(L / p) * p), but never start below p*p, then cross out that multiple, the next, and so on up to R — writing to slot m − L.
approaches.complexityReasoning: Stage 1 sieves up to √R in O(√R log log √R). Stage 2: each base prime p crosses out about (R − L)/p slots, and summing 1/p over primes ≤ √R gives a log log factor, so the window work is O((R − L) log log R). Space is the window O(R − L) plus the base sieve O(√R).
approaches.explanation:
Split the job into two stages. **Stage 1 — base primes.** Run a normal Sieve of Eratosthenes up to `floor(√R)` and collect those primes. **Stage 2 — sieve the window.** Allocate a boolean array `mark` of length `R − L + 1`, where slot `i` stands for the number `L + i`, and assume every number in the window is prime. For each base prime `p`, cross out its multiples that fall inside `[L, R]`. Whatever stays marked is prime.

**Why base primes up to √R suffice.** Take any composite `x` in `[L, R]`. Write `x = a·b` with `a ≤ b`; then `a ≤ √x ≤ √R`. The smallest prime factor of `x` is therefore at most `√R`, so it appears in our base list — and when that base prime sweeps the window it crosses `x` out. No composite can escape, because each has a witness ≤ √R. Primes larger than √R are never needed as erasers; they only ever appear as survivors.

**Why the shift `x → x − L`.** The window doesn't start at 0, so we can't index it by the number itself (that would need an array of size R). Instead slot `i` holds number `L + i`, i.e. number `x` lives at slot `x − L`. Every read and write goes through that offset. Dropping the `− L` is the classic bug — it silently writes out of bounds or to the wrong cell.

**Why the start is `max(p*p, ceil(L/p)·p)`.** We want the first multiple of `p` that is both inside the window (`≥ L`) and not smaller than `p*p` (multiples below `p*p` have a smaller prime factor that already handles them, exactly as in the plain sieve). The first multiple of `p` at or above `L` is `ceil(L / p) · p`, computed as `((L + p − 1) / p) · p` with integer division — no scanning loop needed. Taking the max with `p*p` keeps the start from dipping below where this prime should begin.

**Why `L == 1` needs a special line.** The number 1 is not prime, but it has no prime factor, so no base prime ever crosses it out. If `L == 1`, slot 0 (which represents 1) survives by default and would wrongly be reported. Clear it explicitly. (If `L == 0`, clear slots for 0 and 1.)

**Why it's overflow-safe.** With `R` near `10¹²`, products like `p*p` and the multiple arithmetic exceed a 32-bit int. In Java everything in the multiple computation is `long`; in Python integers are unbounded so there is nothing to guard.
approaches.insight: The segmented sieve is the plain sieve with the eraser set trimmed to exactly what the window needs: primes up to √R. The two ideas that make it work are independent — 'only √R primes can witness a composite ≤ R' (correctness) and 'index by offset from L' (fitting the window in memory). Master the `ceil(L/p)·p` start and the L = 1 edge and the rest is mechanical.

pitfalls: Forgetting the x − L index shift — writes land in the wrong slot or out of bounds.
Sizing the base sieve to R instead of √R — that reintroduces the memory blowup.
Computing the first multiple by looping up from p instead of ceil(L/p)·p — slow when L is huge.
Not clearing slot 0 when L == 1 — reports 1 as prime.
Using int for p*p or multiple arithmetic in Java with R ~ 10¹² — overflow.

edgeCases.behavior: Window has one slot for the number 1; the L == 1 line clears it → empty result.
No base prime ≤ √R divides it, so its single slot survives → [999999999989].
Base primes {2,3}: 8,9,10 all crossed out → empty list, correctly no primes in [8,10].

commonMistakes: Allocating a sieve of size R instead of a window of size R − L — out of memory for large R.
Forgetting to translate number x to slot x − L when marking the window.
Starting each prime's crossing-out by scanning up from p instead of jumping to ceil(L/p)·p.
Reporting 1 as prime when L = 1 because no base prime crosses it out.
Letting p*p or the multiple arithmetic overflow a 32-bit int in Java when R ~ 10¹².

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Indexing the window by the number instead of the offset
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Slot i represents L + i, so number m must be written at m − L. Writing mark[m] indexes far outside the size-(R−L+1) array and throws (or corrupts memory in C-like languages).

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Finding the first in-window multiple by scanning
commonMistakesDetailed.why: Looping m from p upward until m ≥ L wastes ceil(L/p) iterations — catastrophic when L is ~10¹². Compute the first multiple in O(1) with ceil(L/p)·p.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
m = p
while m < L:        # up to 10^12 / p iterations
    m += p
start = max(p * p, m)
commonMistakesDetailed.good: start = max(p * p, ((L + p - 1) // p) * p)  # O(1) ceil(L/p)*p

commonMistakesDetailed.title: Letting 1 leak through when L = 1
commonMistakesDetailed.why: 1 has no prime factor, so no base prime ever crosses out its slot. Without an explicit clear, the survivor scan reports 1 as prime.
commonMistakesDetailed.bad:
mark = [False] * size
# ... cross out base-prime multiples ...
return [L + i for i in range(size) if not mark[i]]  # includes 1
commonMistakesDetailed.good:
mark = [False] * size
# ... cross out base-prime multiples ...
if L == 1:
    mark[0] = True
return [L + i for i in range(size) if not mark[i]]

patternNote: Segmented Sieve over a high window. Reach for it whenever you need primes (or a multiplicative property) in [L, R] with R too large to sieve directly but R − L small. The recipe — base primes up to √R, then offset crossing-out — generalises to segmented totient and segmented smallest-prime-factor tables.
